newsitem.title: USA: Mass. road deaths down despite hike in speed limit.
newsitem.headline: Mass. road deaths down despite hike in speed limit.

text.p: Deaths on Massachusetts roads have declined since the speed limit rose, according to preliminary reports from the Registry of Motor Vehicles.
On Jan. 29, 1996 - two months after President Bill Clinton ended the federal 55 mph requirement - the speed limit rose to 65 mph on more than 400 miles of Massachusetts highways.

While the RMV will not release its official report on 1996 fatalities until May, registry statistican Laurann Paragona said 420 people died on Massachusetts roads last year, down from 444 in 1995 - a 5.4 percent drop.

A 1995 report by the Governor's Highway Safety Bureau indicates that nearly 80 percent of speed-related fatalities occurred on roads with posted limits below 45 mph. Winding roads, rural roads, and narrow roads are where the real danger lurks, suggested Maria Farah, the bureau's spokesperson.
"The problem is very much a community issue," Farah added.
Twenty years ago, speed was an energy issue. In 1974, the federal government imposed the 55 mph limit to alleviate the fuel shortage.
The energy crisis abated, states were permitted to raise the limit on rural roads. Two sections of the Massachusetts Turnpike, both in the western part of the state, went to 65 mph in 1992.
But the speed limit remained a controversial topic on Beacon Hill. In the years before Clinton placed the decision in the hands of governors, the speed limit debate raged in the Legislature.

Former Gov. Michael Dukakis was a vocal opponent of a speed limit hike. His public safety secretary, Charles Barry, estimated during a 1989 public hearing that raising the limit would mean a 17 percent increase in fatalities.
Barry predicted 110 additional deaths the year the roads went to 65 mph. Instead, the 1996 report indicates 24 fewer during the first year.

Rep. Paul Caron (D-Springfield), former chair of the Committee on Public Safety, said automobile safety - seat belts and air bags - has improved so much since the 1970s that he had not expected raising speed limits to be dangerous.
